21171.sourceSearchName: foundations of mathematics foundations of mathematics
21171.title: Foundations of Mathematics
21171.heading: Foundations of Mathematics > Overview Chapter
21171.content: Mathematics becomes coherent when its subjects are understood as layers of one language rather than as isolated collections of formulas. The foundations in this chapter begin with real numbers and legal algebraic operations, turn those numbers into coordinates and functions, and then use limits and derivatives to describe change. Plane geometry supplies the figures that motivate many equations, while vectors and spherical geometry extend the same reasoning into space. Each later topic depends on earlier conventions about equality, order, measurement, and proof.

21172.sourceSearchName: foundations of mathematics foundations of mathematics
21172.title: Foundations of Mathematics
21172.heading: Foundations of Mathematics > Overview Chapter > Numbers and algebraic structure
21172.content:
[[Real Number Algebra and Arithmetic]] establishes the line on which real quantities are ordered. [[Rational Number]]s describe integer ratios, [[Irrational Number]]s fill the remaining positions, and [[Interval Notation]] records connected solution sets. [[Absolute Value]] converts signed position into distance from zero. The [[Laws of Real Number Arithmetic]] explain why expressions may be regrouped or distributed, while the [[Order of Operations]] removes ambiguity from symbolic notation. [[Scientific Notation]], [[Prime Factorization]], and [[Exponent Laws]] then provide practical forms for scaling, divisibility, and powers.

[[Algebraic Manipulation and Inequalities]] turns those laws into solution techniques. A [[Rational Expression]] carries domain restrictions inherited from its denominator, and a [[Rational Exponent]] links powers with roots. Transformations must preserve the original problem: [[Equivalent Equations]] have the same solutions, but a nonreversible step may create an [[Extraneous Solution]]. [[Partial Fraction Decomposition]] reduces a [[Proper Rational Function]] to simpler terms. Inequalities require additional care because multiplication by a negative number reverses order; [[Linear Inequality]], [[Quadratic Inequality]], and [[Rational Inequality]] problems therefore produce intervals, while a [[Two-Variable Inequality]] produces a region.

21173.sourceSearchName: foundations of mathematics foundations of mathematics
21173.title: Foundations of Mathematics
21173.heading: Foundations of Mathematics > Overview Chapter > Coordinates, equations, and functions
21173.content:
[[Cartesian Analytic Geometry]] translates geometric position into ordered pairs. The [[Cartesian Coordinate System]] gives equations a visible form. [[Slope of a Line]] measures directional change, and the [[Linear Equation of a Line]] packages that change with a point or intercept. Slope relations identify [[Parallel and Perpendicular Lines]], while the [[Distance Between Points]] and [[Perpendicular Bisector]] connect coordinates to Euclidean constructions. The [[Circle Equation]] and broader [[Conic Section]] equations show how entire curves can be encoded. Vectors add direction and magnitude; the [[Dot Product]] measures angular alignment and proves identities such as the [[Parallelogram Law]].

[[Polynomial Equations and Factorization]] studies algebraic expressions whose variable powers are nonnegative integers. A [[Linear Equation]] has one first-degree solution, while [[Completing the Square]] leads to the [[Quadratic Formula]] and the [[Quadratic Discriminant]] classifies its roots. For a general [[Polynomial]], [[Polynomial Long Division]] produces a quotient and remainder. The [[Remainder Theorem]] evaluates the special remainder from division by a linear factor, and the [[Factor Theorem]] identifies roots with linear divisors. The [[Rational Root Theorem]] narrows possible rational roots, while the [[Fundamental Theorem of Algebra]] guarantees complete linear factorization over the complex numbers.

[[Function Analysis and Transformations]] makes dependence itself an object of study. A [[Function]] assigns exactly one output to each input in its [[Domain and Range|domain]], and the [[Vertical Line Test]] recognizes that condition on a graph. The [[Absolute Value Function]], [[Exponential Function]], [[Rational Function]], and [[Piecewise-Defined Function]] illustrate different domains and graph shapes. [[Function Composition]] joins rules in sequence; a [[Function Transformation]] shifts, scales, or reflects a graph; and an [[Inverse Function]] reverses a one-to-one mapping.

21174.sourceSearchName: foundations of mathematics foundations of mathematics
21174.title: Foundations of Mathematics
21174.heading: Foundations of Mathematics > Overview Chapter > Trigonometry and local change
21174.content:
[[Plane Trigonometry]] begins by measuring rotation through [[Angle Measure in Radians]]. On the [[Unit Circle]], coordinates become the sine and cosine [[Trigonometric Ratios]], and repeated rotations explain [[Trigonometric Periodicity]]. The [[Pythagorean Trigonometric Identity]] follows directly from the circle equation. [[Angle Addition Identities]] combine rotations and generate the [[Double-Angle Identities]] and [[Half-Angle Identities]]. For general triangles, the [[Law of Sines]] relates opposite parts, while the [[Law of Cosines]] extends the Pythagorean theorem beyond right angles.

[[Limits and Continuity]] supplies the transition from finite algebra to calculus. The historical [[Method of Exhaustion]] anticipates the [[Limit of a Sequence]], where successive approximations approach a fixed value. A [[Limit of a Function]] describes nearby behavior even when the function value at the point differs or is absent. Its two [[One-Sided Limit]]s must agree. [[Continuity at a Point]] additionally requires that common limit to equal the function value. The [[Intermediate Value Theorem]] guarantees that a continuous graph passes through every intermediate height. [[Horizontal Asymptote]] and [[Vertical Asymptote]] describe limiting end or boundary behavior, and the [[Squeeze Theorem]] determines a difficult limit from simpler bounds.

[[Differential Calculus]] converts limits into rates of change. The [[Derivative]] is the limiting slope of secant lines, and the [[Derivative Function]] records that rate across a domain. [[Tangent Line Approximation]] explains differentiability as local linearity. The [[Power Rule]], [[Product Rule]], and [[Quotient Rule]] differentiate common algebraic forms, while the [[Chain Rule]] handles composition and [[Leibniz Notation]] keeps the nested dependencies visible. The [[Derivative of Exponential Function]] and [[Derivative of Logarithmic Function]] reveal the special reciprocal behavior of inverse functions $e^x$ and $\ln x$.

21175.sourceSearchName: foundations of mathematics foundations of mathematics
21175.title: Foundations of Mathematics
21175.heading: Foundations of Mathematics > Overview Chapter > Euclidean and spherical geometry
21175.content:
[[Euclidean Geometry Theorems]] organizes plane reasoning as definitions and proofs. [[Euclidean Axiomatic Geometry]] makes assumptions explicit, after which basic results such as equality of [[Vertical Angles]] and the [[Triangle Angle Sum]] support longer deductions. The [[Isosceles Triangle Theorem]] and [[Triangle Congruence]] transfer equality among corresponding parts. The [[Pythagorean Theorem]] links right triangles to squared lengths, [[Parallelogram Theorems]] organize parallel quadrilaterals, and [[Similar Triangles]] preserve shape under scaling. Circle geometry culminates in the [[Inscribed Angle Theorem]] and the supplementary-angle property of a [[Cyclic Quadrilateral]].

[[Spherical Trigonometry and Spatial Vectors]] shows which plane intuitions survive in three dimensions and which must change. A [[Plane Equation in Three Dimensions]] is controlled by its normal vector, and a [[Sphere Equation]] fixes distance from a center. A [[Great Circle]] is cut by a plane through that center; three of its arcs bound a [[Spherical Triangle]]. The [[Cross Product]] produces a perpendicular vector and area, while the [[Scalar Triple Product]] produces oriented volume. Normals determine the [[Angle Between Planes]], making vector methods suitable for spherical angles. The [[Spherical Law of Cosines]] and [[Spherical Law of Sines]] solve general spherical triangles, and [[Napier's Rules]] provide a compact method for right spherical triangles.

Together, these subjects describe a progression from quantity to structure, from structure to representation, and from representation to change. Algebra makes transformations accountable, coordinates make geometry computable, functions make dependence explicit, limits control approximation, derivatives describe local variation, and geometry keeps the symbolic results tied to space. The recurring principle is preservation: every valid calculation or proof must preserve the relationship being studied while expressing it in a form better suited to the next question.

21181.title: Flight Science
21181.heading: Flight Science
21181.content:
Parent topic: [[Computational Science and Simulation]]

Flight Science is the chapter-level topic for the atmosphere, aircraft, navigation, performance, planning, and operating practices that make controlled flight possible. Full Notes should use one of the focused child topics below rather than linking directly to this chapter tag.

21182.title: Flight Science
21182.heading: Flight Science > Overview Chapter
21182.content:
Flight begins in the atmosphere. [[Atmospheric Thermodynamics and Air Data]] explains how temperature, pressure, density, moisture, and altitude determine the state of the air through which an aircraft moves. Those quantities are not merely environmental background: they determine the speed of sound, the relationship among indicated and true airspeed, the lift available from a wing, and the power and runway length an aircraft requires. Pressure instruments infer motion by comparing static and stagnation pressure, while density altitude translates a combination of pressure and temperature into a practical warning about performance.

The same atmospheric state develops into operational weather in [[Aviation Weather Interpretation]]. Moisture variables describe how near the air is to saturation, and thermodynamic diagrams organize vertical soundings so that cloud bases, instability, convective energy, and inhibiting layers can be recognized. Aviation reports and forecasts then convert observations and predictions into standardized messages. METAR, SPECI, TAF, trend forecasts, SIGMET, AIRMET, pilot reports, and machine-readable IWXXM products differ in scope and urgency, but together they help a pilot understand both current conditions and plausible changes along a route.

[[Aerodynamics and Flight Forces]] connects the atmosphere to the airframe. An airfoil redirects flow and develops lift while also producing drag. Angle of attack controls the aerodynamic state more directly than aircraft attitude, and exceeding the critical angle produces separation and stall. Boundary layers, camber, center of pressure, center of gravity, bank angle, load factor, incidence, and wing twist explain why an aircraft can be stable in one configuration yet approach a limit in another. Straight-and-level flight is only one force balance among climb, descent, glide, and turning flight.

Power for many training aircraft is organized in [[Piston Aircraft Engines and Combustion]]. The four-stroke cycle admits, compresses, burns, expands, and exhausts an air-fuel mixture. The carburetor uses a Venturi pressure drop to atomize fuel, mixture control adapts the fuel flow to changing air density, and the fuel system must remain vented to prevent starvation. Combustion chemistry distinguishes theoretical air, excess air, incomplete products, and adiabatic flame temperature. Horsepower measures and the ideal Otto cycle then connect chemical energy to crankshaft work and propeller output.

[[Orbital Mechanics and Unmanned Flight]] extends controlled flight beyond a crewed airplane. Kepler's laws and conservation of energy relate orbit shape, period, velocity, and escape conditions. Unmanned aerial vehicles add a ground or autonomous control system to the vehicle itself. In a quadcopter, paired rotor directions cancel reaction torque, differential rotor speeds produce roll, pitch, and yaw, and feedback controllers continually reduce the error between commanded and observed motion. Mission design therefore joins mechanics, sensors, communication, mapping, planning, payload, and energy capacity.

21183.title: Flight Science
21183.heading: Flight Science > Overview Chapter
21183.content:
The practical capabilities of an aircraft are evaluated in [[Aircraft Performance Analysis]]. Pilot operating handbook data describe cruise, climb, stall, fuel use, takeoff, and landing under defined assumptions. Regression can summarize those relationships and reveal which variables have a measurable effect, but a fitted equation remains bounded by its input data and the exact aircraft represented. Temperature, pressure altitude, weight, bank, flap setting, and wind all change operational margins, so performance calculation is a disciplined interpretation of approved data rather than a substitute for it.

Navigation begins with position and direction in [[Aeronautical Coordinates and Vector Navigation]]. Latitude and longitude locate points on an oblate Earth, while azimuth, zenith, rhumb lines, great circles, and magnetic variation describe directions that are not interchangeable. Coordinate transformations express the same location in polar, cylindrical, spherical, or Cartesian form. Vector addition then combines true air velocity with wind to produce ground velocity, and inner products provide a route to great-circle distance. Pilotage and dead reckoning connect this mathematics to visible landmarks, time, speed, and distance.

The curved Earth must be represented on a usable surface, which is the problem of [[Aeronautical Chart Projections]]. Scale and conformality determine what a chart preserves. Mercator projection makes a constant-bearing rhumb line straight but enlarges scale away from the Equator. Lambert conformal conic projection makes a great-circle route nearly straight across its intended midlatitude region. Polar stereographic, transverse Mercator, and oblique Mercator projections move the region of minimum distortion to poles, north-south corridors, or a selected route. GEOREF and aeronautical chart conventions give these surfaces a common location language.

Before departure, [[Aircraft Airworthiness and Resource Planning]] asks whether the aircraft is legally and physically ready and whether its limited capacity has been allocated safely. Certificates, logs, inspections, defects, and maintenance intervals establish airworthiness. Weight-and-balance calculations keep mass and center of gravity within approved envelopes, while maximum takeoff, landing, and zero-fuel limits constrain traffic load. Fuel planning separates ramp, trip, contingency, alternate, reserve, and extra fuel, and in-flight monitoring checks whether actual consumption still supports the plan. Radio propagation and line of sight add communication coverage to the same resource picture.

[[Cross-Country Flight Planning and Diversion]] turns those inputs into a route that can be executed and revised. Weather, aerodromes, terrain, restrictions, frequencies, headings, performance, fuel, and loading are assembled before flight. True course becomes magnetic and compass heading through variation, wind correction, and deviation. A filed plan or itinerary supports search and rescue if the flight does not close normally. When circumstances invalidate the destination or route, a diversion establishes a new heading, altitude, timing estimate, and recovery leg while preserving communication and cockpit discipline.

21184.title: Flight Science
21184.heading: Flight Science > Overview Chapter
21184.content:
The moving air mass is treated explicitly in [[Wind Navigation and Flight Range]]. Crosswind and headwind components affect runway choice, crab angle, groundspeed, fuel, and time. Drift can be corrected with double-error or opening-closing-angle methods depending on where the aircraft is along the leg. Point of safe return asks how far the aircraft may continue and still return with available endurance, whereas the critical or equal-time point asks where continuing and returning take equal time. Their different questions make both useful over water, mountains, or any route with few alternates.

The final segment of a flight is organized in [[Instrument Approaches and Glide Planning]]. Precision approaches provide both lateral and vertical guidance; non-precision approaches may require the crew to construct a stable vertical path from altitude, distance, and groundspeed. Constant-descent methods reduce level-offs and exposure to controlled flight into terrain. Rules of three and five approximate top of descent and vertical speed for a three-degree path. Power-off glide planning applies the same geometry to engine failure, where altitude becomes a finite reserve of reachable distance.

[[Aircraft Gyroscopes and Cabin Pressurization]] covers two systems that make flight legible and survivable. Gyroscopes provide stable attitude and heading references through rigidity and precession but accumulate real and apparent wander from friction, Earth rotation, transport, and imperfect compensation. Pressurization maintains a tolerable cabin altitude as outside pressure falls. Outflow and relief valves regulate the pressure differential, climb-rate controls limit discomfort, and the fuselage repeatedly carries hoop stress. Those cycles make fatigue life a structural consequence of operations, not merely calendar age.

[[Global Navigation Satellite Systems]] extends navigation from charts and onboard estimates to a worldwide positioning, navigation, and timing infrastructure. Satellites broadcast synchronized coded signals and orbital data; receivers infer range from signal travel time and solve simultaneously for three-dimensional position and clock bias. Ground control, atomic clocks, augmentation networks, and multiconstellation receivers make that solution useful, while ionospheric delay, unfavorable geometry, jamming, spoofing, and institutional control show why an apparently effortless position fix still requires layered engineering and operational resilience.

Finally, [[Aircraft Conversion and Flight Operations]] shows how these principles meet an actual aircraft and crew. Replacing a piston engine with a turboprop changes power, mass distribution, structure, fuel capacity, wiring, cooling, control surfaces, and certification evidence. Composite fabrication, redundant pumps, leading-edge devices, and digital geometry capture support the retrofit, but every improvement must be reconciled with center of gravity and loads. Flight-test preparation, upper-air safety, crew resource management, and the PACE communication sequence extend the engineering lesson into practice: disciplined flight depends on anticipating the next state and making concerns actionable before they become emergencies.

21185.title: Flight Science
21185.heading: Flight Science > Overview Chapter
21185.content: Together these topics form one operational chain. Atmospheric state produces weather and aerodynamic limits; the airframe and engine turn energy into controlled motion; performance data bound what is possible; charts and vectors define where to go; airworthiness, loading, fuel, and communication determine whether the plan is supportable; and flight procedures continually compare the plan with the aircraft's actual state. Flight science is therefore not a collection of isolated formulas. It is the coordinated use of physics, data, machines, maps, and human judgment to preserve safe margins from preparation through landing.

21200.sourceSearchName: finite element analysis finite element analysis
21200.title: Finite Element Analysis
21200.heading: Finite Element Analysis > Overview Chapter
21200.content:
Finite element analysis converts a continuum problem into a finite system of algebraic equations. A physical domain is divided into elements that meet at nodes, and each node carries a defined set of unknown field values. An interpolation model describes how those nodal values vary inside an element. Local equations relate the unknowns to loads, sources, material behavior, and geometry; assembly then combines every local contribution into a global system. Boundary conditions make the model correspond to the physical problem, and the solved nodal values support recovery of secondary results such as stress, heat flux, velocity, or electromagnetic field intensity.

The algebra behind this process appears in [[FEM Mathematical Foundations]]. Matrices organize element coefficients, nodal variables, and load vectors, while partitioning separates groups such as free and prescribed degrees of freedom. Addition drives assembly, multiplication applies interpolation and constitutive relationships, and transposition forms symmetric energy expressions. Determinants, inverses, Gaussian elimination, and eigenvalue problems provide conceptual routes to static and dynamic solutions. In realistic computation, the structure of a large sparse global matrix matters as much as its formal closed-form solution.

[[Finite Element Method Foundations]] describes the recurring workflow across engineering domains. Discretization selects element size, type, and arrangement. Nodes define degrees of freedom, and shape functions interpolate the unknown field. An element stiffness or characteristic matrix and an element load vector encode local behavior. Assembly maps them into a global equation by shared node numbers. Essential boundary conditions may be imposed through elimination, penalty terms, or multipoint constraints. Once the primary field is solved, derivatives and constitutive equations produce the quantities engineers actually interpret.

Structural examples begin with [[Axial Bar Finite Elements]]. An axially loaded member develops normal stress and strain linked by Young's modulus. A two-node element uses linear displacement interpolation and constant strain, whereas a three-node element uses a quadratic field that better represents distributed loads or changing cross section. The strain-displacement matrix turns nodal displacement into element strain, and equivalent nodal loads represent distributed or thermal actions. Varying-area bars demonstrate why subdivision or higher-order interpolation is necessary when stiffness changes along a member.

[[Truss Finite Elements]] extend axial behavior to networks of oriented members. A planar truss element has two translations at each endpoint, but its physical deformation remains axial. Direction cosines project local extension and force into global coordinate components. Each oriented element matrix is assembled at its endpoint degrees of freedom, so shared joints enforce compatibility and equilibrium. After free joint translations are solved, member stress and support reactions can be recovered and checked against independent joint-equilibrium calculations.

21201.sourceSearchName: finite element analysis finite element analysis
21201.title: Finite Element Analysis
21201.heading: Finite Element Analysis > Overview Chapter
21201.content:
[[Beam Finite Elements]] represent flexure rather than pure axial extension. A planar beam node carries transverse deflection and slope, allowing the interpolation to reproduce both displacement and rotation. The element stiffness matrix relates these degrees of freedom to shear forces and bending moments through elastic modulus, section moment of inertia, and length. Simply supported and cantilever boundaries prescribe different combinations of displacement and slope. Solved deflections lead to internal shear, moment, and bending-stress results.

Thin or longitudinally constrained bodies require two-dimensional continuum models. [[Plane Stress Finite Elements]] distinguishes plane stress from plane strain through the constitutive matrix. Constant-strain and linear-strain triangles, linear quadrilaterals, and isoparametric elements offer different accuracy and geometric flexibility. A plate with a circular hole illustrates symmetry reduction and stress concentration: a quarter model can represent the full structure when symmetry constraints are correct, but the mesh must resolve the steep gradient around the hole. Von Mises stress provides a compact post-processing view, while equilibrium and analytical stress-concentration factors help validate it.

The same assembly logic applies beyond structural displacement. [[Finite Element Heat Conduction]] uses temperature as one scalar degree of freedom per node. Conductivity and geometry form the element heat-conduction matrix, while internal generation and prescribed heat flow contribute load terms. Convection adds both a boundary coefficient and an ambient-temperature contribution. One-dimensional elements can model composite walls; two-dimensional meshes handle interacting boundary conditions and lateral gradients. The solved temperature field is differentiated to recover heat flux.

[[Finite Element Fluid Flow]] focuses on ideal potential flow. Incompressibility, inviscid behavior, and irrotationality reduce the flow to a scalar velocity potential or stream function. Streamlines show the instantaneous velocity direction, while potential derivatives give velocity components. Fluid elements assemble nodal potentials under boundary conditions around bodies such as cylinders and airfoils. This formulation is deliberately distinct from viscous flow, where shear, boundary layers, and no-slip behavior require a richer set of governing equations.

Time-dependent structure introduces [[Finite Element Dynamics]]. A mass matrix represents inertia and a damping matrix represents energy loss in addition to elastic stiffness. Modal analysis solves a generalized eigenvalue problem to obtain natural frequencies and mode shapes. Harmonic response analysis studies sinusoidal forcing near those frequencies, while transient analysis follows response to an arbitrary load history. Boundary conditions, density, mesh resolution, time step, and forcing representation all affect the reported motion.

21202.sourceSearchName: finite element analysis finite element analysis
21202.title: Finite Element Analysis
21202.heading: Finite Element Analysis > Overview Chapter
21202.content:
Electromagnetic problems first require the physical framework in [[Electromagnetic Field Foundations]]. Maxwell's equations and the continuity equation connect fields to charge and current, while constitutive relations introduce permittivity, permeability, and conductivity. Static, quasi-static, source-free, and time-harmonic assumptions produce different simplified equations. Interface conditions determine which tangential and normal components are continuous or discontinuous. The Lorentz force connects fields to mechanical action, and the Poynting vector represents electromagnetic power flow and energy balance.

[[Finite Element Electromagnetics]] then turns that theory into a discretized field solution. Linear line and triangular potential elements approximate scalar fields and their gradients. Variational and weighted-residual formulations derive element equations for Poisson, Laplace, and Helmholtz problems. Waveguide analysis becomes an eigenproblem whose eigenvalues approximate cutoff parameters and whose eigenvectors approximate modal fields. Automatic mesh generation reduces manual preparation, higher-order elements improve approximation through additional nodes, and absorbing boundary conditions permit finite meshes to represent radiation toward an unbounded exterior.

Across every chapter, finite element analysis is an approximation discipline rather than a software ritual. Element selection, mesh resolution, coordinate and unit consistency, material assumptions, and boundary conditions determine what the equations mean. Analytical solutions, equilibrium, conservation, symmetry, and refinement studies provide independent checks. A credible result is therefore not merely a converged solver output; it is a discretized model whose assumptions and numerical behavior have been tested against the physics it claims to represent.

21208.title: Feature Engineering
21208.heading: Feature Engineering
21208.content:
Parent topic: [[Machine Learning and Neural Networks]]

The construction, transformation, selection, and evaluation of representations that make raw data usable for analysis and machine learning.

21209.title: Feature Engineering
21209.heading: Feature Engineering > Overview Chapter
21209.content:
Feature engineering is the work of choosing how observations become variables that a learning system can use. It sits between raw data and modeling: the representation determines which regularities are visible, which comparisons are easy, and which distinctions may disappear. A [[Feature Engineering Foundations|foundational view]] begins with the feature itself—an attribute of a data object—and with the feature vector that collects attributes into a comparable form. Categorical, ordinal, and numerical variables carry different semantics, so their encodings should preserve meaningful relationships. One-hot encoding can remove a false numerical ordering from categories, while transformation, generation, and selection alter the space to make a task more tractable, accurate, or understandable.

The appropriate representation follows the structure of the source data. [[Text Feature Representation]] ranges from strings and edit distance to word sequences, bag-of-words counts, TF-IDF weights, phrases, structural descriptions, and latent semantics. Each level preserves something different: character similarity, token identity, local multiword context, document structure, or co-occurrence patterns. Sparse explicit features remain interpretable, while learned dense spaces can share statistical strength among related expressions. The decision is not merely about dimensionality; it defines what textual evidence a downstream model is permitted to recognize.

Images similarly support several kinds of [[Visual Feature Representation]]. Color histograms and moments provide compact global summaries, correlograms restore some spatial relationship, and co-occurrence matrices or Gabor filters expose texture. Shape context and histograms of oriented gradients describe form through relative geometry and local edge direction. Latent methods such as principal component analysis and Laplacian Eigenmaps instead derive coordinates from the observed image collection. Handcrafted descriptors state an intended invariance explicitly, whereas learned representations adapt to variation in the data and task.

Order creates additional representational choices. [[Time-Series Feature Engineering]] can characterize an entire series through distribution, stationarity, autocorrelation, entropy, or fitted-model behavior; summarize discriminative intervals; or recognize local shapelets and symbolic patterns. These features allow fixed-dimensional comparison among series of different lengths and can also describe where forecasting methods work well. [[Sequence Feature Engineering]] generalizes the pattern idea to ordered symbols and events. A sequence feature combines a pattern—such as a k-gram, closed pattern, or gap-constrained pattern—with a usage rule such as presence, cumulative count, position, or sliding-window activity. Separating the pattern from its mapping prevents mining frequency from being mistaken for the final representation.

21210.title: Feature Engineering
21210.heading: Feature Engineering > Overview Chapter
21210.content:
Some environments make batch construction impossible. [[Streaming Feature Engineering]] addresses observations or dimensions that arrive over time when the complete input cannot be stored. Online principal components, matrix sketches, discriminant projections, manifold approximations, and kernel methods update representations incrementally. When features themselves stream in, selection methods must make sequential decisions about relevance and redundancy under unknown future dimensionality. Statistical controls such as alpha-investing illustrate how an online selector can manage accumulated false discoveries rather than treating every arrival independently.

Relations among objects require a graph-aware space. [[Graph Feature Engineering]] includes neighborhood counts, egonet structure, global position, and recursive aggregation of neighbor properties. Graph embeddings replace named measures with dense coordinates learned from network proximity. DeepWalk and node2vec use random-walk contexts, while GraRep factorizes relationships at several transition lengths. These methods do not preserve “the graph” in a universal sense; each objective selects a particular meaning of structural similarity, so the learning target should guide the representation.

Once candidates exist, [[Advanced Feature Selection]] controls irrelevance, redundancy, cost, and risk. Filters score data properties without repeatedly fitting a chosen model; wrappers evaluate subsets through model performance; embedded methods select as part of fitting. Search can be complete, sequential, randomized, or expressed through sparse optimization. Modern settings add requirements beyond accuracy: a subset may need to remain stable under resampling, reconcile multiple views, protect private statistics, or resist features that an adversary can manipulate. Selection is therefore a statement about operational constraints as well as predictive association.

[[Automated Feature Engineering]] turns construction into a guided search. Unary and binary transformations can be composed into a transformation graph whose nodes represent derived datasets. Expansion-reduction systems generate broadly and prune; evolutionary systems mutate and recombine candidate representations. Performance-guided traversal, reinforcement learning, distribution-based utility, and transformation recommenders allocate a limited evaluation budget. Automation expands the search that can be attempted, but its transformation vocabulary, validation design, and reward signal still encode human assumptions.

[[Pattern-Based Feature Engineering]] offers a structured version of construction. Frequent- or contrast-pattern mining defines candidate motifs, a selection phase controls redundancy and relevance, and a mapping function converts each match into binary, frequency, confidence, or growth values. The resulting pattern space can feed an ordinary classifier or become the basis of clustering. Keeping mining, selection, and mapping distinct is important: a common pattern is not automatically discriminative, and a useful pattern can behave differently under different value mappings.

21211.title: Feature Engineering
21211.heading: Feature Engineering > Overview Chapter
21211.content:
Neural methods learn representations through training objectives rather than fixed formulas. [[Deep Feature Representation]] includes restricted Boltzmann machines, deep belief and Boltzmann networks, autoencoders, convolutional transfer, word embeddings, and variational autoencoders. Reconstruction, probabilistic modeling, contextual prediction, and supervised transfer each preserve different information. Bottlenecks, sparsity, corruption, and latent priors keep a learned feature space from becoming an uninformative copy. A deep representation is useful because of the constraints and evidence that formed it, not simply because it has several layers.

Application chapters show why domain structure remains indispensable. [[Social Bot Feature Engineering]] combines profile, friend, interaction-network, content, sentiment, and timing evidence because automation is behavioral and relational, not a single account flag. Holistic, pairwise, and egocentric detection choose different units of analysis, while Botometer demonstrates a broad operational feature system. [[Software Analytics Feature Engineering]] transforms code metrics, development history, change entropy, diffusion, commits, text, and developer activity into evidence for file-level or just-in-time defects, crash-prone releases, and turnover. Time-aware construction is essential so that future outcomes do not leak into present predictions.

Finally, [[Twitter Feature Engineering]] integrates short text, user profiles, structured metadata, media, and networks for platform-specific questions. Profile classification, crisis intent, and location estimation emphasize different subsets of those signals. Spatio-temporal-thematic analysis connects what is discussed with where and when activity occurs. Across every domain, the central lesson is consistent: a model sees only the distinctions its features make available. Effective feature engineering therefore combines data structure, task requirements, computational limits, and evaluation discipline into a representation whose strengths and omissions are explicit.

21244.sourceSearchName: engineering geometry modeling engineering geometry modeling
21244.title: Engineering Geometry Modeling
21244.heading: Engineering Geometry Modeling > Overview Chapter
21244.content:
Engineering analysis begins before a solver sees an equation. It begins with a geometric representation that decides which dimensions, boundaries, features, and relationships exist in the model. [[Engineering Geometry Foundations]] supplies the vocabulary for that representation. Points, lines, curves, planes, surfaces, angles, coordinate systems, topology, and symmetry describe both shape and connectivity. Form, fit, and function then connect the representation to its purpose, while dimensional choice and optimization determine how much of the physical object must be retained.

A production CAD model and an analysis model serve different goals. CAD often preserves manufacturing detail, assembly relationships, and exact product definition; finite-element geometry must also form valid domains, support a useful mesh, and expose stable entities for physics. [[CAD and FEM Geometry Exchange]] covers the translation between these environments. Native kernels can preserve rich geometry and associativity, while neutral formats exchange a smaller common representation. Repair tolerances reconcile nearly coincident vertices and short edges, but overly aggressive repair can silently change the shape. Imported scale, units, topology, and boundaries therefore require deliberate checks.

Interoperability can extend beyond a single import. Live links propagate parameter changes from CAD into analysis, and multistage workflows transfer fields or tabular results from one solver into another. These conveniences do not remove responsibility for interface meaning. Every transferred quantity needs a coordinate frame, unit convention, entity mapping, and physical interpretation that the receiving model can preserve.

Once the domain enters COMSOL, [[COMSOL Geometry Configuration]] establishes its modeling context. Space dimension, axisymmetry, physics interfaces, study type, length and angular units, geometry kernel, and default repair tolerance all influence which operations and equations are available. The Model Builder tree records how global definitions, components, geometry, materials, physics, mesh, studies, and results relate. Parameters and variables replace anonymous dimensions with reusable definitions, while automatic rebuilding can keep dependent geometry current during controlled changes.

[[COMSOL Geometry Operations]] turns primitives and imported bodies into analysis-ready domains. An ordered geometry sequence makes construction reproducible. Transforms copy, move, rotate, reflect, scale, or array objects. Boolean operations unite, intersect, subtract, or compose them, and partitions create regions needed for different materials, meshes, or boundary conditions. Conversions change how lower- and higher-dimensional entities are represented. Virtual operations alter the way meshing interprets topology without changing the underlying CAD object. Work planes support profile construction, extrusion, revolution, sweeping, and cutting, while named or rule-based selections keep entity assignments stable as geometry changes.

21245.sourceSearchName: engineering geometry modeling engineering geometry modeling
21245.title: Engineering Geometry Modeling
21245.heading: Engineering Geometry Modeling > Overview Chapter
21245.content:
The extended-surface examples in [[Parametric Fin Geometry]] demonstrate how those tools cooperate. One-, two-, and three-dimensional fin representations expose the tradeoff between computational cost and retained physics. Rectangular, cylindrical, pin, radial, channeled, webbed, curved-profile, and twisted fins can be built from parameters, profiles, work planes, partitions, deletions, and composite domains. Parameterization makes dimensions auditable and enables systematic comparison, but geometry alone does not establish performance; thermal fields and integrated heat flows must still evaluate the shape.

[[Simulation Geometry Quality]] closes the workflow by asking whether the representation is trustworthy and economical. Physics-preserving simplification removes detail that does not affect the investigated behavior. Defeaturing suppresses holes, rounds, slivers, and spikes that degrade meshing, while symmetry and dimensional reduction remove repeated or negligible regions only when loads, materials, and boundary conditions permit. Build diagnostics reveal disconnected or overlapping entities, stable selections protect physics assignments, and measurement checkpoints catch unit or scale mistakes after import.

Quality is not maximum detail. Mesh, geometry extent, and parameter sweeps should show when reported quantities become insensitive to further refinement. The law of diminishing returns then redirects effort from cosmetically perfect geometry toward assumptions that materially affect the decision. A credible engineering geometry is therefore not the most elaborate available model; it is the simplest representation that preserves the relevant physics, survives reproducible checks, and remains understandable across the software interfaces that use it.
